description: We are Dhruvion, a team of curious builders, developers, and space enthusiasts passionate about turning ideas into impactful solutions. We bring skills in AI/ML, data, software development, research, and creative problem-solving. Join us if you love exploring the unknown, collaborating with motivated minds, and building technology that can make a difference on Earth and beyond. 🚀
summary: DHRUVION is a Martian mapping and mission-planning platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 challenge, “Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map". It brings planetary surface information and terrain analysis into a unified web-based interface to help users explore the Martian landscape and understand factors that can influence mission planning. The project uses NASA planetary data resources, including MOLA elevation data and Mars surface imagery, as its data foundation. Built with React, TypeScript, Leaflet, FastAPI, NumPy and Rasterio, DHRUVION connects an interactive frontend with geospatial processing capabilities. Its goal is to make Martian terrain information more accessible and support informed exploration and route-planning decisions. DHRUVION is a prototype and does not certify route safety or replace professional mission analysis.
details:
DHRUVION – Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map

1. The Problem: Making Martian Exploration More Informed

Human exploration of Mars presents a complex challenge: every mission must make decisions about where to travel, which regions to explore, what environmental conditions to consider, and how to manage limited time and resources in an unfamiliar planetary environment.

Unlike exploration on Earth, Martian missions cannot depend on continuous human assistance, conventional infrastructure, or immediate access to ground support. Rovers and future human explorers must operate with incomplete observations, communication delays, uncertain terrain conditions, and strict mission constraints.

Although NASA and other planetary science organizations provide extensive Mars datasets, these resources are distributed across different instruments, archives, formats, coordinate systems, and scientific documentation. Understanding how elevation, surface characteristics, imagery, environmental observations, and radiation measurements relate to a specific exploration scenario requires considerable technical effort.

DHRUVION addresses this challenge by bringing relevant Martian geospatial and scientific information into a unified, interactive mission intelligence platform.

2. Our Solution: DHRUVION

DHRUVION is an interactive Martian terrain exploration and mission intelligence platform designed to help users investigate the Martian surface and make more informed exploration decisions.

Our initial focus is Gale Crater and Mount Sharp, one of the most scientifically significant exploration regions on Mars and the location of NASA's Curiosity rover mission.

DHRUVION combines planetary terrain visualization, scientific dataset integration, environmental information, route-planning capabilities, and an AI-assisted interaction layer.

Rather than simply displaying a map, the platform is designed to transform scientific observations into understandable information that can support mission exploration and planning.

Its central objective is to connect three elements:

  • Explore: Understand the Martian landscape through interactive geospatial layers.
  • Analyze: Interpret terrain and available scientific observations using data-driven processing.
  • Plan: Evaluate exploration routes and mission constraints through computational tools and an intelligent interface.




Figure 1. Orbital view of Gale Crater and Mount Sharp, the primary exploration region selected for DHRUVION. Image credit: NASA.







3. NASA Data: The Scientific Foundation

DHRUVION uses real NASA and USGS planetary data, processed and organized into a structured dataset package specifically for the Gale Crater area.

Four primary data categories have been prepared:

A. MOLA – Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter

MOLA provides elevation information derived from Mars Global Surveyor laser altimetry.

The supplied dataset includes:

  • Elevation in metres above the MOLA areoid.
  • Derived slope in degrees.
  • Derived terrain roughness using the Terrain Ruggedness Index (TRI).
  • A spatial coverage mask identifying usable and restricted cells.

The terrain products use an approximately 463.09-metre grid with 410 × 410 cells.

Slope was derived using the Horn method, while terrain roughness was calculated using the TRI method described by Riley et al. (1999).

These layers provide a regional understanding of elevation changes and surface characteristics that can inform preliminary route assessment.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"Gale Crater" ]

B. CTX – Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter Context Camera

The CTX dataset provides a reduced-resolution mosaic of Gale Crater at approximately 50 metres per pixel.

It serves as a visual surface reference for exploring the region and placing terrain information into geographical context.

The imagery is associated with documented spatial bounds and is displayed using a Mars-compatible equirectangular coordinate system.

Its actual coverage is preserved; areas outside the imagery footprint are not represented as observed imagery.

CTX pixel values are Digital Numbers (DN), not calibrated surface reflectance.

Figure 3. Grayscale orbital Context Camera mosaic showing Gale Crater, its rim, and central layered mound. Image credit: NASA.













C. REMS – Rover Environmental Monitoring Station

REMS measurements from NASA's Curiosity rover provide historical environmental observations.

The supplied package contains measurements from sols 9 and 11, including:

  • Air temperature.
  • Ground temperature.
  • Atmospheric pressure.
  • Relative humidity.
  • Ultraviolet measurements.
  • Wind measurements where sufficient valid observations exist.

These observations can support historical environmental visualizations and help users understand the types of environmental conditions measured during rover operations.

Figure 4. REMS instruments aboard NASA's Curiosity rover used to measure environmental parameters including temperature, pressure, humidity, and ultraviolet radiation. Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech.





D. RAD – Radiation Assessment Detector

The RAD dataset provides historical radiation dose-rate observations from Curiosity's early mission, covering sols 1–3.

It includes separate measurements from:

  • Detector B – silicon detector.
  • Detector E – plastic scintillator detector.

The original measurement unit, µGy/h, is preserved, and the two detector series are kept separate.

Together, these datasets establish a scientific foundation for terrain exploration, environmental awareness, and mission-oriented analysis.

Figure 5. Radiation Assessment Detector aboard the Curiosity mission, providing measurements that help characterize the radiation environment on Mars. Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/SwRI.






4. How DHRUVION Works

DHRUVION follows a modular data-to-decision architecture.

Step 1 – Data acquisition and preparation

Planetary datasets are acquired from NASA and USGS resources, organized into raw and processed directories, and accompanied by metadata, source references, validation records, and processing documentation.

Step 2 – Geospatial processing

Terrain rasters are processed using Python, Rasterio, and NumPy. Elevation, slope, roughness, coordinate systems, spatial bounds, and coverage are maintained as structured geospatial information.

CTX imagery is prepared with its associated map bounds and overlay metadata. REMS and RAD observations are organized into clean observation records and statistical summaries.

Step 3 – Interactive exploration

The web application brings the available information together through an interactive Martian map and mission-oriented dashboard.

Users can explore the Gale Crater region, understand available terrain layers, examine imagery, and access relevant scientific observations.

Step 4 – Computational mission intelligence

The backend is designed to support terrain analysis, hazard assessment, route comparison, mission feasibility evaluation, and return-to-base assessment.

Numerical and geospatial calculations are handled by deterministic Python services rather than being left to a language model to invent.

Step 5 – AI-assisted interaction

DHRUVION's AI assistant is designed to let users interact with the platform using natural language.

It can act as an intelligent interface to supported backend tools, helping users request terrain information, understand available observations, compare mission options, and interpret computational results.

The AI layer is intended to explain evidence and limitations, while the underlying scientific calculations remain traceable to their data sources and algorithms.

5. Technical Architecture and Tools

DHRUVION uses a modular full-stack architecture.

Frontend

  • React and Vite for the application interface.
  • TypeScript for structured application logic.
  • Tailwind CSS for responsive styling.
  • Interactive geospatial visualization using the project's map technology.

Backend

  • Python for scientific and computational processing.
  • FastAPI for REST API development.
  • Pydantic for data validation and structured responses.
  • NumPy and Rasterio for numerical and raster processing.
  • NetworkX for graph-based computational capabilities where applicable.

AI and Intelligence

  • A tool-oriented AI architecture for natural-language interaction.
  • Python services for deterministic geospatial calculations.
  • Configurable language-model integration, with Ollama as a local model option.

Data and Deployment

  • GeoTIFF for raster terrain information.
  • GeoJSON and structured JSON/CSV files for geospatial and observational information.
  • GitHub for source-code collaboration and version control.
  • Vercel and Render for frontend and backend deployment.

6. What Makes DHRUVION Different?

The central innovation is the integration of different planetary information types into a single mission-oriented experience.

Instead of treating elevation maps, surface imagery, environmental measurements, and radiation observations as isolated resources, DHRUVION organizes them around the needs of exploration.

Its design emphasizes:

Multi-layer planetary awareness: Multiple scientific data products can be explored in geographical context.

Explainable analysis: Terrain measurements, units, coverage, sources, and processing methods remain identifiable.

Mission-oriented intelligence: The architecture connects exploration data to route and mission-planning workflows.

AI-assisted accessibility: Natural-language interaction can make complex planetary information easier to query and understand.

Scientific transparency: Missing data, uncertainty, spatial restrictions, and measurement limitations are treated as important information rather than hidden.

7. Validation, Reliability and Scientific Integrity

Data quality is essential when building tools intended to support planetary exploration.

The supplied data-processing package includes:

  • 16 candidate datasets catalogued.
  • 4 primary datasets processed: terrain, CTX, REMS, and RAD.
  • 36 raw files ingested.
  • 8 files validated.
  • 29 processed output files.
  • 26 automated data-pipeline tests passed.

The validation process includes raster checks, coordinate reference system verification, metadata inspection, PDS label checks, missing-value handling, unit preservation, provenance tracking, and consistency checks between RAD labels and observations.

The system also preserves important scientific restrictions.

For example, MOLA terrain products have approximately 463-metre spatial resolution and are suitable for regional assessment, not rover-scale obstacle avoidance. CTX imagery has partial coverage. REMS observations cover only sols 9 and 11, while RAD observations cover sols 1–3.

Historical rover measurements are therefore not presented as live environmental conditions or as measurements for arbitrary locations across Gale Crater.

Twelve additional catalogued datasets were not acquired and are explicitly identified as unavailable. No simulated observations are presented as real NASA measurements.

8. Intended Impact

DHRUVION aims to make planetary exploration information more accessible, understandable, and actionable.

Its potential users include:

  • Students and educators studying planetary science.
  • Researchers exploring Martian terrain and scientific datasets.
  • Space enthusiasts interested in planetary exploration.
  • Developers and researchers building planetary mission-planning tools.
  • Future exploration teams investigating data-driven approaches to mission preparation.

By connecting real planetary observations with computational analysis and an accessible interface, DHRUVION provides a foundation for more informed exploration and scientific learning.

9. Future Scope

DHRUVION is designed as an extensible platform.

Future improvements can include higher-resolution HiRISE and rover-scale terrain datasets, expanded THEMIS and CRISM integration, additional environmental and radiation observations, improved terrain hazard models, multi-objective route optimization, autonomous mission replanning, and more advanced AI-assisted mission workflows.

As additional validated data becomes available, the platform can expand beyond its initial Gale Crater demonstration region.

Conclusion

DHRUVION aims to bridge the gap between planetary science data and practical exploration intelligence.

By combining authentic Mars datasets, geospatial processing, interactive visualization, computational mission-planning architecture, and AI-assisted interaction, the project provides a foundation for exploring not only what the Martian surface looks like, but also how available scientific information can support decisions about exploring it.

DHRUVION – Explore the terrain. Understand the data. Plan the mission.
